doc.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998

title: Army camp segregation, then befriending Armstrong and Lucille Wilson
summary: Avakian saw Eldridge with Krupa and was turned away from Armstrong's dressing room, then recalls playing him a test pressing and the ice cream visit with Lucille Wilson.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: It wasn’t just in the south either, was it? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

No it was I understand pretty much everywhere, but worse in the south of course. That’s a period where I was in school so I didn’t observe that particularly. I never saw Billie on stage with Artie Shaw for example, but I did see Roy Eldridge performing in person with Gene Krupa and there was always a little bit of a stir when Roy came down front to do a vocal duet with Anita O’Day. People would say, “Hey look at that, look, he’s going to sing with her. Well that’s pretty damn naive. Of course we guys who were interested in jazz were completely cool about all that, but it was funny to see what would happen. And even — well I shouldn’t say even because this went on for a long time — in the early 40s when I was in the southern Army camp and I was a private at the time in Basic Training, Louis Armstrong came down to the Army camp town I should say, and I went to the performance which was in a dance hall actually. And I was sent upstairs with all the other white people who wanted to hear Louis, and the black audience stayed downstairs. And then I went down and said I would like to say hello to Mr. Armstrong in the dressing room, and there was a beefy cop there who told me what did I want do that for, boy. And I said well he’s a friend of mine. And that was a terrible mistake. Well I mean he didn’t beat up on me or anything but he looked at me with such disgust. He said, “Well you can’t go there. Beat it.” And so I didn’t get a chance to say hello to Louis, whom I knew slightly of course. But we had become very good friends because when I started the research for the Hot Jazz Classic series on Columbia, one of the early things that I discovered was a whole batch of unreleased Armstrongs and I identified most of the personnel quite easily, but one of them I only could detect about four musicians that I could recognize, including Earl Hines of course and so I took the test pressing to New York when I knew that Louis was playing at the Apollo Theater and he invited me to come backstage. I first was told he was in the Braddock bar having lunch with his friends. And he said, “Come on backstage, I’ve got a phonograph.” I didn’t realize at that time that he carried a little portable wind-up machine with a — he always had a tape recorder and record player with him after that once the electrical equipment was developed, and he listened to the record and boy was he happy. He says oh this is wonderful, yeah, that’s Stump Evans and that’s so-and-so, that’s the Carroll Dickerson orchestra. And from that moment on he took a great liking to me, and I remember very shortly afterwards I dropped in on him in New York again, and he said, “Hey, let’s go get some ice cream and we’ll pick up my darling.” And I didn’t know what he meant by his “darling,” because he was married at the time to Alpha, but they were in the process of breaking up. And this darling turned out to be Lucille Wilson, who was the last Mrs. Armstrong and his widow eventually, and he got a quart of ice cream, vanilla ice cream, and we took it to Mrs. Wilson’s apartment, her mother, and Lucille was a dancer at the Lafayette Theater. And I found out later that she had broken some new territory because Lucille was darker than © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
most of the chorus girls. That color business always held forth in the black night clubs in Harlem. They wanted light skinned girls.

That’s it, the bronze-skinned beauties, sepia beauties, and all the — what’s the word, not cliches, the subterfuge type words, I can’t think of the exact word but you know what I mean. And so we enjoyed the ice cream there and Louis polished it off, he was amazing, he had about two-thirds of that quart of ice cream himself. And from that time on, he treated me almost like a member of his musical family. And I remember as we left the house he went down about three or four steps from the apartment and I was parked right in front there, and before he got in the car he stood at the top of the steps and did a little pirouette. And he said, “Oh my God my darling, my darling, she’s so sweet, my darling.” And I thought my God, Louis Armstrong is revealing his inner soul to me, a student.

Oh it was terrific. I realized then that Louis really liked me, and our friendship lasted forever. He used to call up and say, “Hey I’m laying off a couple of days, come on out to the house and bring your brother with you,” because he loved my brother too.
